newsitem.title: USA: Chase, Citicorp Q4 earnings on target.
newsitem.headline: Chase, Citicorp Q4 earnings on target.

text.p: Chase Manhattan Corp and Citicorp, the two largest U.S. banks based on assets, Tuesday reported fourth-quarter earnings close to expectations and showing business continues profitable despite continued slippage in U.S. credit cards.
Analyst Raphael Soifer of Brown Brothers Harriman noted that for now loss rates in the credit card business are being covered by credit card profits.
He said with loss rates above five percent in a growing U.S. economy, the concern is what the losses would look like if the economy slipped into recession.

Regarding Citicorp, ranked second in size with $281 billion in assets, Goldman, Sachs & Co analyst Robert Albertson observed that the credit card business actually improved from the third quarter of 1996 with help from the card business overseas.

Citicorp said net income in the worldwide card business was $290 million in the fourth quarter, a decrease of 20 percent from the fourth quarter a year ago but an increase of 19 percent from the third quarter of 1996.
Citicorp said a closely watched barometer, the chargeoff rate on U.S. bankcards, rose to 5.45 percent of average managed loans in the fourth quarter from 5.11 percent in the third quarter.

Chase Manhattan said its credit card charge off rate in the fourth quarter rose to 5.11 percent of managed receivables from 4.95 percent in the third quarter. The receivables are predominantly from business in the U.S.

Salomon Brothers analyst Diane Glossman said Chase's credit card business was "deterioarting less quickly than most of the other credit card banks." She said loan quality has not been an issue at Chase although there has been a bit of softness in revenue generally.

Paul Mackey, analyst at Dean Witter Reynolds, said Citicorp has achieved a "superb balance" in its business with consumer activities earning $575 milllion in the quarter and corporate banking earning $549 million. He said there was also a good balance between domestic and overseas business.
Glossman, referring to Citicorp, said "the good news is that the growth and profitability in international operations is helping make up for deterioration in U.S. card profitability."
George Salem, analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattison, raised his rating on Citicorp to buy from hold, and set a $130 share price objective.
Salem noted that Citicorp met or exceeded all of its financial goals in the quarter. Citicorp had a 20.6 percent return on equity in the quarter.
At Chase, the return on equiy excluding merger costs was 18.1 percent.

Walter Shipley, chairman and chief executive of Chase, said ln a statement that the banking holding company had an "excellent" quarter and year "led by strong earnings across the full breadth of our businesses."

Chase's net income in the fourth quarter of 1996, before merger costs, rose nine percent to $901 million from $827 million in the fourth quarter of 1995. Before the merger costs, fully diluted earnings per share were $1.88 compared with $1.73 in the year-ago quarter.

Chase, which was formed when Chemical Banking Corp acquired the old Chase Manhattan in 1996 and re-named itself the new Chase Manhattan, said it had merger savings of $235 million in the latest quarter.
Citicorp chairman John Reed said in a statement that the company "continued to produce strong financial results with excellent returns."

Both Chase and Citicorp repurchased shares in the quarter. Chase said it repurchased $1 billion of its common equity during the quarter. Citicorp said it repurchased 8.1 million shares of common at a cost of $820 million in the quarter.
Citicorp, which raised its quarterly dividend to $0.525 per share from $0.45, was up 1-7/8 to 111-1/8 in afternoon trade.
Chase Manhattan was off 5/8 to 92-1/4.
